speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND THE APPLICATION OF THE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned for lunch I was talking about the compensation provisions under Bill C-28. The present method of compensation for livestock owners who have animals which are condemned because of disease provides a fixed amount of compensation. In some cases, on top of this the owner is able to realize the salvage value of the animal. However, this varies a great deal depending on the circumstances and whether the animal can go for food purposes or whether it has to be condemned for food purposes. Under the bill before the House, the livestock owner will be compensated to the fair market value. It seems to me that this method of compensation is much more fair to the livestock owner.
Also, there is provision in the bill for compensation for fodder or feed which has to be destroyed because of the diseased condition of the animals on the premises. I think the committee should look at other aspects when a complete herd must be depopulated and income is curtailed for short periods of time. This is something which requires much more study, but I think the committee will want to look at the idea of making provision for this in the act. At some time in the future it may be deemed advisable to write regulations in this regard. That is not to say that the livestock owners do not have a responsibility. It seems to me that they have a responsibility, when purchasing animals, to take adequate precautions related to sanitation and disease.
Good assistance is available from the Health of Animals Branch with regard to the testing of samples of blood or whatever biologic is used to examine the animal for disease. The bill also clarifies many parts of the existing act which perhaps are not as clear as they should be in light of the existing health programs and disease control programs which are now in effect in the country today. These relate to the designation of areas for disease control. There is further clarification of definitions such as concerning animals, birds, bees and domestic animals which are covered by this act, as well as veterinary biologies which have been covered previously, but the terminology is further outlined.
I think one of the important parts of this bill relates to the section concerning deadyards and rendering plants. In the past year we have had a great deal of publicity in this country concerning dead animals which were diseased finding their way back to the human food chain. This bill makes provision for the regulation of deadyards and rendering plants right to the construction, operation and

maintenance of animal deadyards and rendering plants and the regulating of packing and marking of products of deadyards and rendering plants. Surely this is a very important addition to our health of animals program and further identifies the reason for changing the name of the bill, which refers to animal and human protection, as well as the infectious aspect of the bill.
Another aspect which is covered by the bill is the regulation and control of semen for artificial insemination purposes. Surely this is a very important aspect of Canada's export program. I understand that two million vials of semen are exported to some 30 different countries each year. It is important that there be control of diseases which might be spread in this manner.
I think it is important to recognize how much progress has been made in the control of disease in humans and animals because of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act over the years. Some 40 years ago, the program for control of bovine tuberculosis was initiated and it has been very successful in controlling the disease in cattle and in humans, too, because the disease often came from the reservoir within domestic animals.
In the past few years, a great deal of progress has been made in the control of brucellosis in cattle. This is called undulant fever in humans. In 1951, 8 per cent to 10 per cent of our cattle population was infected with brucellosis, with an annual loss, in terms of milk and calves aborted, of some $9 million. By 1956, as a result of the vaccination program, infection from brucellosis in the cattle population was reduced to 4.5 per cent. The test and slaughter program started in 1957 and the first testing was completed by 1966. The effect of the program can be seen in the reduction of the infection to .2 per cent of the total cattle population of 15 million. This is a dramatic success story.
As one who was engaged in the practice of veterinary medicine when the program was introduced, I must say I was a Doubting Thomas. I did not think a disease as infectious as brucellosis could be handled so effectively through a test and slaughter program, as tuberculosis had been in previous decades. That is not to say that we do not have infected herds in Canada today; obviously, with a .2 per cent rate, there are still some. It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and his advisers in the Health of Animals Branch will have to decide in the next year or so whether to go completely for the test and slaughter program or continue with vaccination.
I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) support the idea of the complete elimination of the Calflood vaccination program. I think this is the direction we should move in, and that the continued vaccination, although it may be encouraging and useful to the individual cattle owner, is not as useful in the over-all picture of disease control in Canada. Continued vaccination only complicates the testing procedure and masks infection in animals. I hope in the next year or so the government will move to discontinue the vaccination program which some provinces still encourage. If we do eliminate vaccination, I think we will have to provide a more extensive compensation program, especially when a
October 31, 1975

complete herd is depopulated and the owner's income curtailed.
I believe that the people who administer the Animal Contagious Diseases Act are among the unsung heroes of the public service in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and should be congratulated. Thanks to them, we have one of the most healthy and active livestock exporting countries in the world. They make it possible for us to trade in livestock with 120 nations around the world. They are one of the most important factors of our livestock industry. I believe this bill will strengthen the powers of the government to carry out the contagious diseases aspect of the work of the department and the new area of protection of animals in transit, as well as the other aspects of public health.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND THE APPLICATION OF THE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to participate in this debate on the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. The hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) indicated that Canadians have little appreciation of the bill, and I think that is quite true. If we were confronted with an epidemic of undulant fever, tuberculosis or foot and mouth disease, as in 1952, the case would be different. The bill is important, however, and deserves the attention of this House. Therefore, I am pleased to add my comments.
I was interested in the minister's opening remarks when he reviewed the history of the bill. I am sure he would want me to add one or two points to what he said. The bill was introduced in 1869, as he indicated, but I think he would like to know that was the first agricultural bill introduced in this House, and it was introduced by the Conservative government under Sir John A. Macdonald.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND THE APPLICATION OF THE ACT
speechtext: With the co-operation of the opposition.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND THE APPLICATION OF THE ACT
speechtext:
And we are interested in co-operating with the government on this bill, which we believe is excellent in principle although we have reservations about certain aspects of it. I want to deal in a general way with the bill and then come to some of the specifics, particularly the transportation section, which is new. The bill has been introduced as a vehicle to maintain the country free of serious animal diseases and to eradicate those that can be eradicated and bring under control those that cannot be eradicated.
The minister earlier indicated some amendments to the act. These are in regard to regulations which existed in the past: they are questioned as to their validity at the present time. I think we must realize this is an important feature of the bill before us. In addition, we have a new section dealing with transportation-clauses 31 to 34. I will deal with them in more detail in a few seconds. I am concerned about the issue of regulations. I have mentioned my concern in the past. In effect, the operative part of the bill cannot be analysed by the House, nor in committee. I saw the same situation earlier this week in connection with the environmental contaminants bill and the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act.
The operative parts of this particular bill cannot be analysed in detail. I agree that orders in council are important and must be introduced from time to time. In cases
Animal Contagious Diseases
where regulations are to be enacted-and I strongly suggest that the government will enact many regulations affecting the operative parts of the bill-I suggest that those regulations should be made known to members of the House so that those who are interested in and affected by the bill will be aware of the regulations when the bill is approved by the House. I suggest that a mechanism should be established to this end. This would remove some of the apprehensions of some hon. members, and some individuals who will be affected by this type of legislation. I suggest that the minister should seriously consider amending the bill in such a way as to enable people more readily to assess the impact these regulations will have on them in the future.
The hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) spoke this morning about evidence taken before the Senate agriculture committee in connection with Bill S-2. In this regard, the presentations made by Mr. Charles Gracey of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, and Mr. C. G. Munro, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, to the Senate Standing Committee on Agriculture on April 24,	1974, are germane. Mr. Gracey stated in
testimony:
While we support the obvious intent of sections 31 and 32, we cannot state unconditional support for the various clauses, in ignorance of the regulations alluded to but not stated.
I think the presentations made before the Senate agricultural committee are relevant to the present debate and it will be useful to summarize and perhaps paraphrase a portion of the testimony relating particularly to sections 31 and 32. Generally, the regulations relevant to those proposed sections ought to embody two fundamental principles. First, the regulations ought to ensure the safe and humane transportation of livestock. Second, they should promote maximum efficiency and speed in livestock movement. As the minister knows, total time spent in transit has a most important bearing on the welfare of livestock, but this matter has not been defined in the act and is not defined in the bill.
I suggest that proposed new section 32 will need to be considered carefully in committee. The discussion will interest many who are following the progress of this bill. Proposed section 32(1), on page 14 of the bill, proposes regulations-
-requiring, in such circumstances as may be prescribed, the examination of animals before being loaded on board any aircraft, railway car, vehicle or vessel for transport.
This section clearly refers to the preloading examination of animals. Where there is general agreement that animals should be loaded in good condition, excessive regulations may be impractical and have an adverse effect. At present, cattle originate from more than 150 points in western Canada and there is an obvious need to clearly define the regulations and the inspection procedures contemplated by the government.
Second, to a great extent there is a built-in safeguard in the routine transportation of cattle in that livestock producers buying feeder stock in the west are very conscious of needing to load animals in safe condition. Proposed section 32(b) proposes regulations-

October 31, 1975
Animal Contagious Diseases
-respecting the transportation of animals affected with or suffering from an infectious or contagious disease or incapacitated by reason of age, infirmity, illness, injury, fatigue or any other reason-
Again, it is possible to support in principle this subsection, but the language and implications are such that a more thorough examination of the regulations will be necessary in committee. Proposed section 32(c) proposes regulations-
-establishing the area to be allocated to each animal being transported in relation to the mode of conveyance-
Again, this is an extremely important section and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association have been advocates of "safe loading levels" for various sizes of cattle. This principle should be given careful consideration in the formulation of regulations. A point frequently repeated is the importance of air space, which may be as critical as floor space if decks are too low. If there is to be a standardization in terms of area per animal, it becomes necessary to have the breakdown into various sizes and weights of animals. We should pursue this in committee. Proposed section 32(d) proposes regulations-
-requiring animals to be segregated during transport according to class, age and sex-
This section refers to regulations with respect to segregating livestock as to class, age and sex. Again, it is necessary to ascertain if in fact the proposed regulations are practical and within the spirit of the legislation. Bulls should not travel loose with females, otherwise the major consideration should be size and weight. For example, while it is not common practice to move steers and heifers in the same car, provided their weights are uniform there is in fact no hazard to such movement and arbitrary regulations prohibiting such movement would be undesirable. Proposed section 32(e) says that the governor in council may make regulations-
-requiring any railway company or the operator or owner of any aircraft, vehicle or vessel, when engaged in the transportation of animals
(i)	to disinfect and clean any aircraft, railway car, vehicle or vessel that such company, operator or owner uses for the transportation of animals, and
(ii)	to maintain any facilities for the loading and unloading of animals, including such rest and feeding stations as are necessary-
We recognize the importance of this section and, indeed, I have had representations from sheep producers in my area regarding inadequate care in some yards. In this regard, there are sheep producers who maintain that sheep in transport will fare much better if they are shipped straight through rather than being unloaded within a specified time. There is an obvious necessity to define the specific regulations dealing with disinfecting and maintenance of facilities. New subsection 32(f) calls for regulations-
-(f) specifying the standards of care of animals, including the provision of feed and water during transit, that are to be observed by any railway company or the operator or owner of any aircraft, railway car, vehicle or vessel when the company, operator or owner is engaged in the transportation of animals;
This is another extremely important section dealing with standards of care of animals during transit. Such regulations should be understood by all parties, and because of the obvious importance to shippers and receivers their practical experience should be considered in the formula-

tion of regulations. New section 32(g) calls for regulations-
-establishing the maximum number of hours that animals may be transported in any particular means of conveyance without being unloaded for rest, feed and water-
This is an extremely important section which requires careful examination of the proposed regulations. As the minister knows, section 404 of the Criminal Code establishes 36 hours as the maximum time in transit that animals may be loaded in cars without being offloaded for rest, feed and water. The first point that must be made is that the inclusion of the present section in this bill and its removal from the Criminal Code is indeed a positive step. The second point is the difficulties and dangers in establishing the maximum number of hours in transit. Surely the major consideration should be the safety and humane treatment of livestock. I suggest very strongly that if the only consideration is "X" number of hours, invariably the emphasis will shift from one of humane transportation to one of enforcement of a regulation. Of course, this may well not be in the interests of the stock.
As the minister undoubtedly knows, there are variances between cattle, hogs and sheep in their ability to withstand prolonged periods in transit. I also believe that from the investigators' studies to date this particular issue has not been resolved. We are, therefore, anxious to review this aspect of the regulations regarding time in transit, acknowledging the importance of safety and humane treatment but questioning the benefits of the stated number of hours.
The final point of this section is the delayed time in transit due to the poor co-ordination of transportation systems. I have no intention of getting into the whole area of the transportation system, but I think it is important to note that such a cargo as stock should be considered as a priority project. In this regard, it should receive very special attention by the transportation system. I suggest that this very simple measure would add substantially to the well-being of livestock that are in transit. Subclause (h) reads:
(h)	establishing, where animals are unloaded for rest, feed and water, the minimum number of hours that may be allowed the animals for those purposes-
Again, the emphasis is related to the minimum number of hours for rest, feed and water. Therefore, it will again be necessary to assess the specifics of the regulations. Earlier, I mentioned receiving a representation regarding inadequate care of sheep during offloading. I was surprised and somewhat shocked to learn at that time that herds of sheep arriving in my constituency from the west had been abused on offloading, with obvious injuries and, indeed, with death of the stock at times. Although it is not clear in the language of the bill that it is covered, surely the intent of the legislation would call attention to this particular problem in some demonstrable fashion. Subclause (i) reads as follows:
(i)	establishing the manner in which stalls, containers, pens and fetter-ings in aircraft, railways cars, vehicles or vessels used in the transportation of animals shall be constructed, equipped and maintained.
October 31, 1975

Again, there is no objection to regulations for construction standards, providing the intent is for the safe and humane treatment of livestock. However, there is a risk in government circles to promote uniformity for the sake of uniformity. Of course, we will be very anxious to assess the proposed standards and determine if in fact they are in keeping with the intent of the legislation.
I have dealt in some detail with clause 32 because it is a new and extremely important feature of this bill. I have also attempted to demonstrate the difficulties experienced on this side by interested parties who will be involved in assessing such a bill without a draft form of the regulations or some indication from the government or the department as to what the regulations may include. I certainly recommend to the Standing Committee on Agriculture that there be a clause calling for the establishment of an advisory committee of appropriate groups to assist in the formation of regulations which will apply to the transportation sector.
Before turning from this new and important section on transportation, it should be noted and emphasized that the legislation allows for transportation of all animals. We will obviously be interested in the minister's proposals for the transportation of animals for research purposes, the regulations which will be required for the containing and handling of a large variety of animals, the recommendations regarding the safety and well-being of the animals, as well as the protection of aircraft from unnecessary and dangerous contamination from natural wastes and infectious and contagious micro-organisms. We will also be interested in knowing the priorities which will be established for the transportation of animals, the types of facilities at airports envisaged under this legislation, and the training of personnel associated with the care of animals in transit. I would simply say, with respect to this entire section on transportation, that there are numerous areas we will pursue in the standing committee. I am sure we will have the co-operation of the minister in pursuing these particular avenues.
I want to make a few comments on those parts of the bill that extend to surveillance and increase the mechanisms to keep reportable and non-reportable contagious or infectious diseases in check. Again, I wish to indicate my general support for these measures, but as I interpret the legislation there appear to be some inconsistencies in the penalties. I seriously question whether the desired results will be obtained with some of the restrictive features. I refer to page 8 of the bill, clause 6, which reads as follows:
"9. (1) Every owner of animals and every breeder of or dealer in animals, and everyone bringing animals into Canada shall, on perceiving the appearance of any reportable disease among the animals owned by him or under his special care, give immediate notice to the nearest veterinary inspector of the Department of Agriculture of the facts discovered by him as aforesaid.
This clause implies that the average producer should have the ability to recognize on sight all of the reportable diseases defined in the act or subsequently defined by the minister. With all due respect, I seriously doubt whether the average breeder could pronounce the 26 diseases listed in the act, let alone diagnose their presence. I suggest that the present legislation is unrealistic and the associated penalty excessively severe.
Animal Contagious Diseases
Clause 6 continues:
(2) Every veterinarian in Canada shall, immediately on ascertaining that an animal has a reportable disease, give notice of the existence of the disease to the nearest veterinary inspector.
In my view, this should be more closely interrelated with the previous subclause. During the examination of miscellaneous estimates on November 28 of last year, I asked what I considered to be a very key question as it relates to the total problem of control of contagious and infectious disease. I inquired as to the communication that exists between the veterinary inspectors and the department and the practising veterinarians. The answer clearly indicated there is no line of authority in transmitting this information to the professionals in the field, the veterinarians. At that time Dr. Wells had this to say:
We are, however, developing now and we hope to have very shortly the first issue of a publication which will go forward from the health of animals branch to all practising veterinarians in the country and this will list areas in which these diseases are found.
It is not my intention at this time to list instances in which reportable diseases have been present in a district and where the practising veterinarians have had no knowledge of its existence, but I wish to emphasize in the strongest terms possible that this practice is wrong and is not in the best interests of controlling infectious diseases.
I have no difficulty in accepting the principle that this is a confidential matter between the owner and the Department of Agriculture. But surely there is an overriding principle here, and that overriding principle must be the dissemination of information rapidly and accurately to the professionals responsible for the care of animals. Medical ethnics dictate that the present practice should stop and common sense makes it clear that all practising veterinarians must be involved in the control of infectious and contagious diseases. I want to tell the minister that I will actively pursue this matter when the bill is before the standing committee.
I want, now, to turn to the area of compensation which has been alluded to by other hon. members in this debate. The principle that I believe should be embodied in the legislation should be that of replacement value. Again, I suggest that the minister give consideration to establishing a mechanism whereby there is participation by those affected in developing and updating regulations to conform with changes in the industry. The section of the bill dealing with compensation is a very important one. It is an area I have discussed on many occasions with my colleague, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), and he certainly shares the view that the market value approach is an improvement. However, I know he feels it would not be satisfactory or as equitable as compensation payments made on the basis of replacement value. If this latter approach could be adopted, particularly for dairy cattle, by using a reasonable base price figure plus an index formula dealing with breed, age, type classification and production records or potential, I know the hon. member feels there might be a much more accurate and acceptable form of compensation payment.
I know the hon. member for Elgin has met with dairy producers in Ontario and that he has in his possession proposals based on this particular theory prepared by Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
October 31, 1975
Animal Contagious Diseases
Arnold Stansell in co-operation with the joint dairy breeds organization. The Minister of Agriculture and many members will recognize Mr. Stansell as one of North America's most successful breeders of Ayrshire cattle. It is my intention and the intention of the hon. member for Elgin, when the bill is before the committee, to request that he have the opportunity of appearing as a witness to explain this proposal in detail to all members of the committee.
On November 27, 1974, the minister officiated at the opening of the Animal Diseases Research Institute and graphically described the 1952 experience with foot and mouth disease. As I indicated at the outset, for this type of debate perhaps we need this kind of experience to generate interest in the importance of this legislation. The minister described at the time the cost in terms of cattle lost, taxpayers' money spent to eradicate the disease, loss of exports of livestock and livestock products for a full year, resulting in a bill totalling approximately $900 million. That experience is a constant reminder of the necessity to have legislation that will keep this country free of serious animal disease and to eradicate those diseases that remain with us.
In light of this, during the examination of the Supplementary Estimates B, 1974-75, on November 28 of last year I made reference to the problem of Johne's disease which, to my knowledge, has affected at least four herds in my area. As part of the testimony, Dr. Wells, the veterinary director-general, Health of Animals Branch of the department, stated:
Mr. Chairman, in accordance with the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, all infectious and contagious diseases are reportable. However, the specific list of diseases that are in the act and listed as main diseases are these for which we have national programs such as brucellosis, tuberculosis, hog cholera, foot and mouth disease, where action is taken to eradicate the disease from the country. In the case of Johne's disease, it is an infectious and contagious disease, and therefore reportable, and if the owner wishes to have the infection cleared up, we are prepared to provide the program to that owner.
If and when the time comes that a better system of eradicating the disease comes about, and when we can clear some of the problems facing the department with respect to disease, it may be possible to move into a national program with respect to Johne's.
I want to emphasize that it is my impression that in my area this disease is highly contagious, consisting of what appears in many instances to be a virulent organism. Responses to my questions at that time indicated that the method of treatment is herd eradication, which is similar to the procedure adopted for brucellosis and tuberculosis. It seems to me that if the minister is desirous of retaining an animal health status that is the best in the world in his view, then Johne's disease should be added to the list of diseases outlined in the bill. Again I ask the minister to give serious consideration to this particular program and to see that it is pursued during the study of the bill by the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
During the same meeting, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) and I raised the very serious and important question concerning income tax on moneys received for herds destroyed as a result of brucellosis, tuberculosis or Johne's disease. As the minister knows, if these herds are not replaced in the same calendar year, then the money received from the government by way of compensation is taxed. I am well aware that it is the government's intention to encourage the farmer to reinvest these sums in

establishing his herd, but in many instances this is impossible to accomplish in the calendar year. For example, the lapse of time between the slaughter of the herd and the procedures that must be followed to ensure a healthy environment, free of disease, for housing the new herd may well extend beyond the calendar year, and in many instances the replacement animal that the farmer wants, particularly in the case of dairy herds, cannot be procured during the calendar year. I know the minister is concerned about this problem, and on November 28 he indicated that he was negotiating this point with the departments of national revenue and finance. Since this is an important component of the compensation problem, I urge the minister and the government to correct this present inequity before the bill receives third reading. I know we will be anxious to pursue this point at the committee level.
In conclusion, let me reiterate that we support the importance of this piece of legislation, and I commend the minister and the department of their interest in maintaining healthy animals in Canada. But again I re-emphasize that we believe the present bill can be substantially improved and I have attempted to define some areas of concern regarding various components. We will also be making some constructive proposals during committee stage. Finally, may I say it is our intention to work in a positive manner and as rapidly as possible to implement the improvements I have suggested.

Mr. Speaker, before I make a few comments about this particular bill I should like to refer to something the minister said just before lunch when he introduced the measure. He alluded to what I am sure was the foot and mouth disease outbreak in Regina and the tremendous loss that took place back in 1952. Let me say to the minister and his staff who are here in the House of Commons at this time that his words took me back very vividly to that time. The minister spoke about the tremendous cost to this country. He did not put a dollar value on it, but somebody behind me mentioned $1 billion. It could well have been that amount. Even if it cost that much to clean up the outbreak, I would suggest that is peanuts-and I mean it-compared to the loss in inventory value to the cattle industry in Canada at that time.
In October, 1951, fed cattle and feeder cattle were selling for $35 and above-at that time the highest price by far in our history. I can remember selling feeder yearlings going at 800 pounds for $36.20 a hundredweight. That foot and mouth outbreak occurred when an immigrant whose first name was Willie came over to that Regina farm and threw out some dried-up sausage. Within a few days the value of the cattle dropped by half. Fed cattle dropped to $18 a hundred and feeder cattle to about the same. It was a great loss. I only remind the minister about this to show the tremendous importance of the Health of Animals Branch to the Canadian economy as a whole. His remarks took me back a few years and prompted these opening comments.
By and large, this is a good bill in that it updates many obsolete portions of the act. It incorporates many new developments, procedures and techniques that are now part of our total Canadian livestock industry. Perhaps the most critical thing I could say about the bill at this time is that it is two years overdue. I suggest that the minister

must, surely, take the blame for this. The tragedy is that agriculture apparently has such a low priority on the legislative ladder and the order paper of the House of Commons.

speechtext:
I want to make some opening comments on the transportation aspects covered by this bill. First of all, I should like to again commend the government and the minister for transferring the authority for the transportation of livestock from section 404 of the Criminal Code to the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, under the Department of Agriculture. This is an excellent move and is long overdue.
Most of my remarks will relate to the movement of cattle, especially from western Canada, to so-called central and, occasionally, far eastern Canada. I want to refer, first of all, to a very important brief that was presented to the government back in 1973, entitled "Statement on Livestock Transportation". Even though it was presented on January 17, 1973, I think portions of it are very applicable today. Therefore, I should like to quote from it briefly.
The brief was presented to Hon. Otto Lang, then minister of justice, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). It was put together by a joint committee of the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association and the Ontario Beef Improvement Association, with the assistance and co-operation of Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway. I shall read just a short part of it as follows:
Our purpose is to seek the creation of the type of federal legislation which will permit development of a more efficient and humane system for transporting livestock and specifically feeder cattle. It is our view that the Criminal Code is not the most appropriate legislative vehicle for legislation of this kind. What is required, we submit, is legislation that will control the conditions under which livestock are transported, while at the same time providing sufficient safeguards to satisfy public concern.
Later in the statement we read the following:
Our interest, therefore, is to speed the cattle to final destination as quickly as is reasonably possible and to do so requires some progressive amendment to the Criminal Code.
The statement continues:
We were well pleased with the experience in 1972, and the non-stop run from Winnipeg to Toronto and points beyond brought with it many benefits.
The total elapsed time in transit was reduced in many cases.
Because cattle were kept moving, the rail and stockyards system was less burdened with backlogs and delays.
Rail cars were tied up with one load for a shorter period of time and availability of cars was a less crucial problem.
I think that last point represents the most practical advantage of the faster runs which started back in the fall of 1972. The statement ends with four recommendations which I think are still most important and I propose to read them:
We respectfully wish to close our statement with the following recommendations.
1.	That the Minister of Agriculture be requested to establish a special committee to develop guidelines for the humane, efficient transportation of livestock.
2.	That the committee be formulated to include representatives designated by the railways, the producer organizations (i.e. Canadian Cattle-
Animal Contagious Diseases
men's Association and the Ontario Beef Improvement Association) and the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies.
3.	That new legislation based on these guidelines, governing the transportation of livestock, and to be administered by the Canada Department of Agriculture, be developed and introduced as soon as is practically possible.
4.	That the procedures for shipping cattle employed in 1972 be repeated in 1973.
Although these recommendations are outdated, they refer to prior runs of non-stop shipments of livestock from Winnipeg through to Toronto. The report is dated January 17, 1973, and now, almost three years later, we are just getting around to making these recommendations part of the act.
I think there are special comments on rail and truck movement of calves to Ontario which need to be made at this time. I might add that these comments are based on my personal experience of well over 25 years. During that period I have been associated with cattle sales at Walsh, in southeastern Alberta. On average during those 25 years we loaded and shipped 25 to 50 carloads-sometimes more-of calves and feeder yearlings per sale to Ontario points. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt) was the auctioneer at most of those sales, so he knows very well what I am referring to now.
The greatest concern of Ontario buyers always has been the risk of death, and sickness losses. These are sometimes very expensive. At times these deaths number from 3 to more than 20 animals in a car. This represents a considerable loss. If the animals are not dying, very often the sickenss is considerable and it takes weeks and even months to get over such a loss. Our experience over the years as producers and shippers of feeder calves and yearlings would suggest the following: first, we should load only healthy animals, subject to veterinarians' visual inspection. We should watch for signs of fever, pneumonia and scours, to name only a few.
Calves should not be shipped the day they are weaned if at all possible. As a matter of fact most of them are shipped the day after they are weaned. Second, calves should be offered water before loading on to the stock cars. I think that is most important.
Third, and of the utmost importance, is the fact that the total time in transit, which includes any rest stops, should be kept to a minimum. I think what I should like to stress more than anything else about the shipment of calves from the prairies to Ontario is that the total time in transit should be kept to a minimum.
Fourth, one feeding and water stop only in Winnipeg should be necessary. This implies that a non-stop route from Winnipeg to Ontario designation points should be a reality.
Fifth, a further implication is that the old 36-hour release regulations be changed to at least 48 hours. I hope this specific item will be discussed with the cattle producers in western Canada, with the feeders and buyers from Ontario, as well as with the railway people when that decision is formulated in the regulations. It is well known that a reduction in the total time in transit means that sickness loss can be dramatically reduced. The Winnipeg-

October 31, 1975
Animal Contagious Diseases
Toronto non-stop run is now reasonably well accepted, but this amendment to section 31 and section 32 is needed for the final authority.
Still on the matter of transportation I wish to make a plea for a speed-up of railway modifications at Midhurst, Ontario, north of Toronto, to facilitate the transfer from railway to trucks and hence to the final destination. This, I am told, will bring about further savings in time and, of course, increased efficiency. This Midhurst decision made by the CPR sometime ago for some reason or other has seemed to have bogged down, and it was only recently that work started again. It is doubtful if it will be completed this fall so as to be availabe for the heavy run of feeder cattle which is now well under way. That heavy run of cattle traditionally amounts to something like 300,000 head every fall in modern times. Some years ago it was much higher. I suggest that the railways have a definite responsibility here in having vastly increased the livestock freight rates.
I think it is appropriate to point out here that another rate increase has now been indicated in livestock rates to be effective November 14. Since January 1 of this year, since the freeze was lifted, the cumulative increases in respect of livestock rates have reached 64.4 per cent for single-deck livestock cars and 86.9 per cent for double-deck livestock cars. This is what the increases will be when this last increase becomes effective on November 14. I think there is an obvious aside I should make. Surely the government's new restraint program should be involved in this.
I wish now to refer to an excellent editorial in the Cattlemen. This is the October issue. The editorial is headed "Railways Should Try Harder". It states:
The railways have a poor reputation for moving feeder cattle. That message came through loud and clear when we researched the West-End trucking-story for this issue.
A sample of the comments: 'The railways just don't care about the cattle business'; 'You can't talk to anybody there; they all pass the buck'; 'The railways could do a much better job.'
Cattle shippers complained about shortage of equipment and wrong allocation of cars. That has a familiar ring to observers of the grain shipping system. But behind these impressions are some examples of real hardship. Extra time in delivering cattle costs producers money. Although some changes have been made recently in Ontario, more must be made to reduce time from ranch to feedlot.
Cattle cannot be treated like bulk cargo. The railways know this. It's just amazing that both CN and CP Rail have done so little to adjust their cattle shipping systems to the demands of feeder cattle transport.
Rates cannot be an excuse for this situation. Rates on double deck 40' livestock cars from Winnipeg to Toronto have increased 49.4 per cent since last December. Rates on single deck cars moved up 43 per cent over the same period.
These figures include the extra rate increase that is coming.
Truckers have now had a taste of the business at these new rates. It's time producers received the benefits of real competition in this area.
As a further aside I might add in respect of that editorial that it seems obvious that the railways are making changes in their livestock rates without the danger of a ceiling being imposed on them, such as is the case with statutory grain rates. The result is rather obvious.
I wish to say a little more about the newer aspects of livestock transportation which is now becoming more important, such as the trucking of cattle over long distances, for instance, from the prairies and even from Brit-

ish Columbia to Ontario. There is a definite increase in this movement. Right now approximately 2,000 head a week are being trucked from the west to points in Ontario. This is the greatest volume ever handled in this way. The delivery time of from 50 to 55 hours from Alberta to Ontario is impressive indeed. That represents about a day and one-half to two days faster than shipment by rail. This again promotes the health of calves and reduced losses although the rate is higher. The rate is approximately $1 higher per loaded mile but there are advantages, especially in time saved, which more than compensate for this.
I should like to commend the truckers for their enterprise in this regard and hope that they will meet their 10 per cent objective in respect of the total cross-country haul. Before leaving the subject of transportation I should like to make a comment about what is an annual situation almost every fall. I refer to the shortages of livestock cars for shipment from west to east. This occurs every fall. I feel this could be helped by two factors. One is the shorter turn around made possible by the non-stop run by rail from Winnipeg to Toronto. The other, of course, is the competition by trucks and the faster turn around also made by the trucking industry.
Now I believe it is appropriate to make some practical comments, as a practising cattleman, about the brucellosis controversy. We have heard much about this over the last year. I should say that these are my comments as a rancher from western Canada. I will go back a few years to the time when the program started.
The vaccination program was introduced in 1950 when we had an infection rate of 8V2 per cent. By 1957 through the use of this program the rate dropped to 414 per cent. Finally by 1966 after the completion of the first general test and slaughter program the rate decreased to .02 per cent. This was quite an accomplishment.
Then the period 1968-1969 was the start of what has been called the de-emphasis of the vaccination program. In this connection I want to recall again one of the factors relating to that vaccination. We were finding out, when we were shipping out vaccinated calves, that those which were vaccinated with strain 19 used in calfhood vaccination had a tendency to be stressed far more than other calves which were not vaccinated. While we were anxious to follow the program that was laid down in co-operation with provincial and federal programs, we developed a feeling against vaccinating calves just before they were loaded into stock cars for eastern Canada, and we were relieved when this de-emphasis program came into being.
I am sure that the use of strain 19 before the calves were loaded into stock cars has contributed to increased losses and strain factors that resulted in sickness. We are now moving through the so called withdrawal symptoms of the whole brucellosis program as we shift to a final clean up. My understanding is that it is the government's intention to try to discontinue calfhood vaccination by the end of 1976 when it is assumed that the vaccine will be outlawed permanently.
It is unfortunate there has been some split in the veterinary profession over this issue. There seems to have been a division between some of the private practitioners and

October 31, 1975

some Health of Animals veterinarians. In many instances private veterinarians have supported the vaccination program in this withdrawal period and they are hoping that it will continue. One can only feel that perhaps sometimes their feelings in this regard are dictated by rather short term considerations. Also, what I think are unfair comparisons have been made with the brucellosis situation in the United States, where it is my understanding that the situation is considerably worse than here in Canada.
My own personal view is that the Health of Animals policy of test and slaughter is the right one and the only one. We have to live with that policy. We can never completely eradicate the disease by vaccination, and surely our objective must be complete eradication. I want to say that I fully support the consistent and long range policy of Health of Animals on this matter.
Now I should like to make a few comments about another subject that has made the news recently. I am referring to the disease blue tongue. The minister recently made an announcement calling for a double test of all cattle imported into Canada from the United States for the disease blue tongue. I know from personal representation that this has caused concern with some U.S. exporters of breeding stock to Canada. I know of some from the state of Montana who have been exporting excellent breeding stock to Canada for many years and who feel that it will almost put an end to that type of specialized breeding program. It will also affect the imports of U.S. feeder cattle coming to Canada, but on balance this is a very small quantity. Because of other tests required and the nuisance value of these tests, in total there is very little likelihood that the volume of feeder cattle coming into Canada will be significant.
I am assured by department officials that there is no blue tongue in Canada in either sheep or cattle, and following on newspaper reports of reactors to blue tongue in southern Saskatchewan I must say I was relieved to be informed that all of those that were found to be reactors were imported cattle from the U.S. and were detected and slaughtered. So again I say it is reassuring to note that there are no infected herds in Canada.
I am told that the decision to call for a double test was arrived at after appropriate consultations with animal health officials from Washington. Of course this is the way it should be. It was considered necessary to protect our own status and our trade avenues, not only for the protection of our own industry in Canada but to assure sheep producers in Australia and New Zealand that our trade avenues with them would be protected.
I want to make a brief comment about warble control. The warble control program in western Canada is well advanced thanks to the excellent co-operation among the provinces, the producers, and the federal government. There has been real progress in western Canada although I am sorry I cannot report about eastern Canada, but I am sure there is equal progress there. This was made possible because of the new systemic insecticides. I mention this only to call for continued support of this policy, which mostly involves the provinces, and I hope that the environmentalists here will not get any ideas against the use of this excellent insecticide.
Animal Contagious Diseases
I want to switch to another topic now which caused a great deal of concern in the House and in all of Canada early this spring. I am referring to the dead meat scandal which took place in Quebec and even overflowed into Ontario. I hope it is not a dead issue, and no pun is intended. I want to repeat what I said at the time of the scandal when it made the headlines day after day.
In those provinces that have provincial and federal meat inspection under our Health of Animals Branch-and this includes most of our provinces-I feel very strongly that it should be the responsibility of the senior government, that is, the federal government, to ensure that all meat sold for human consumption is adequately inspected by some level of government. I am saying that the federal government should co-ordinate this important function, I am not suggesting that it should do it all. Surely the ultimate authority should be that of Canada's Department of Agriculture to ensure the program is properly co-ordinated. In making this comment I hope that the regulations are not so severe as to limit or prohibit the operation of the small town or rural slaughter houses. I say this since their most severe critics are their own neighbours who have to be their customers, and such outlets would not dare sell bad meat.
In closing I want to commend the federal government for its support of our three veterinary colleges and their recent special financing. I want to draw attention in particular to the excellent work of the western veterinary college, the Saskatoon college, and especially their work on calf scours and respiratory diseases. I think they should be commended for this. I know they have had additional financing from the federal government and from the cattlemen themselves who have put up a generous amount of research money for that college. In the animal research departments of these institutions and other federal institutions I have been told there is some concern about the proper authority to deal with the increasing use for animals for public research. Ultimately, of course, it is for the good of the general public. I am not sure whether or not this bill covers this item, and if it does not perhaps it could be covered because this is a most vital part of any research.
The amendment of the agreement with France for a second maximum security staging on the Island of Miquelon is noted with considerable interest. It suggests three things. First, it suggests that exotic import interest is continuing and will likely continue, in the opinion of the government, in spite of the currently depressed national commercial cattle industry. Second, it suggests that Canada must have made a good deal with the government of France to get this service. This is not surprising in view of the value of trade that will come through that security station. Third, it suggests that there are good long range indications of continued and even improved export relations with the United States cattle interests in exotics, since it seems to me that a good many will come through our station and then go to the United States.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I want to say that I fully support the broad concept of the bill. I commend the minister and the Health of Animals branch for their courtesy in holding advance consultation with representatives of Canada's cattle industry, humane societies, and the railways for the background needed to bring this bill to its

October 31, 1975
Agricultural Marketing Act
present point. I sincerely hope this will continue in the development and promulgation of the regulations that will be so important in its implementation.
In 1952 I had the privilege of meeting the present Director General of Veterinary Services when he was in charge of the outbreak of foot and mouth disease. It has been my good fortune to maintain an excellent association with him over the years, and I hope it may continue. I look forward to having the bill in committee for examination in detail.

speechtext:
that Bill S-10, to amend the Feed Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Madam Speaker, I should like to introduce second reading of Bill S-10, an act to amend the Feeds Act, as passed by the Senate on March 6, 1975, and as read for the first time in the House of Commons on March 10, 1975. Since the bill was not a money bill and since there was a backlog of legislation in the House of Commons, Bill S-10 was introduced directly into the Senate and received intensive study before being passed.
The feed industry in Canada does approximately $llA billion worth of business annually, and is the sixteenth largest industry in Canada. It employs approximately 10,000 persons and produces about nine million tons of feed each year for use by livestock producers in this country.
The present Feeds Act provides for the regulation of livestock feeds as to composition, packaging, and labelling. The provisions of the act include requirements for registration of feeds prior to sale and other measures designed to prevent the marketing of feeds that are not known to be consistent with current nutritional and health standards for livestock. This form of regulation also prevents feeds from causing adulteration of meat products used for human consumption.
The last major revision of the act was made in 1960. As most hon. members realize, there have been many advances in animal nutrition since that time, as well as in manufacturing, distribution, and testing of feeds. There are many new products now used in feeds that are not included under the present definition of feed and hence are not subject to regulation. Bill S-10 extends the definition of feed to all those products and ingredients used or able to be used, in livestock feeding. However, the new definition of feed is not intended to bring veterinary drugs subject to the Food and Drugs Act, or products subject to the Pest Control Products Act, under its control.
The definition of livestock has also been expanded to include fish, because fish are now being raised by commercial farmers for human consumption.
There is increasing evidence that the public interest or that of the feed users cannot be adequately protected with respect to feed quality without regulation in some situations at the farmer or mixer level. Just as with meat quality, effective regulation must involve plant inspection and regulations applying to the manufacturing process itself. This is necessary to prevent harmful adulteration of meats, for example, which may not be easily detected in time in the finished product.
Feeds can be carriers of disease-causing organisms, such as salmonella, and act as a reservoir for reinfection of animals. Eradication of such infections cannot be accomplished by checking feed for sale only. It is important that manufacturing plants be inspected and clean-ups be done. The changes proposed in Bill S-10 will give authority to
October 31, 1975

inspect manufacturing plants and to require certain levels of sanitation.
In passing this bill, the Senate made an amendment regarding penalty clauses. Perhaps, hon. members will recall that the former minister of justice, the Hon. Otto E. Lang, reported to the House of Commons on March 27, 1975, that in his opinion this amendment was inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of the Canadian Bill of Rights. I am happy that this opinion was expressed because it is important that all legislation be consistent with the provisions of the Bill of Rights. I would ask that this amendment be dealt with by the Agricultural Committee of the House of Commons when this bill comes before it.
I note that there was a good deal of discussion about pet foods in the Senate debates on the bill. I would simply say that pet foods have not been named as such in this bill. It will be noted that feeds for any species of livestock have not been named either. The definition of livestock provides the opportunity for pet foods to be brought under the act.
I may say, in conclusion, that the proposed changes have been supported by the various sectors of the feed industry affected by this act. My department held extensive discussions with trade, universities, colleges, and producer groups during the drafting of this bill, and I can report that those sectors directly affected are in agreement with the bill as originally submitted to the Senate.

Madam Speaker, my comments on the bill will be brief. The bill is short, and basically we support its contents. I understand that the Canadian Feed Manufacturers Association which represents some 400 feed manufacturers transacting business to the approximate value of $1.5 million, supports and welcomes this bill. Basically this amending bill is designed to protect livestock producers and consequently consumers of livestock. Technological changes of the past ten years have made it necessary to introduce these amendments, to cover some of the chemical substances and exotic matters fed to livestock.
I note that the definition of livestock has been widened to include fish, rabbits, and mink, and such other creatures as may be designated by order in council or regulation. One wonders why pets such as cats and dogs were not included in the regulations. Their inclusion was suggested when the matter was debated in the Senate. I understand that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is reluctant to see pets included in the definition, as it is felt that it would take considerable manpower and staff to supervise the pet food industry. I ask the minister to consider amending the bill in order to include pet foods under the regulations. It is important to ensure the high quality of pet foods fed to pets in this country, in order to avoid health hazards to our population.
I note, from reading the debates of the other place, that the Senate spent some time considering the penalty provisions. I will not comment on these at this time, but we reserve our right to consider them in committee. I do not anticipate that this bill will take too much time in committee.

speechtext:
That Bill C-25, an act to protect human health and the environment from substances that contaminate the environment, be amended in subclause 5(3) by striking out line 18 at page 8 and substituting the following therefor:
"(3) Any person, except his cause of objection is shown to be unreasonable, frivolous or vexatious"
He said: Madam Speaker, there is a principle involved here that has to do with who can participate in bringing into play the provisions set out regarding environmental contaminants in the Canadian environment. There is a general principle that it is going to be important to have as broad a participation as is possible in questions relating to possible contamination of the Canadian environment. The disagreement has to do with the legal interpretation of a word. The word that appears in the bill limits the right to participate to those persons who have an interest.
Our concern is that the word interest is subject to very narrow and specific legal definition, such as would mean only a legal interest, excluding two categories of people we believe should not be excluded. First, it would exclude that very large although perhaps undefinable portion of the Canadian public which can be called the environmental public, those Canadians worried about environmental questions. They are often very well-informed about the potential dangers to the environment that can arise from specific actions. Our concern is that this language would not allow a member or an organization in the group broadly called the environmental public to engage in proceedings under this bill unless they had a specific legal interest that was being affected. We believe that is too narrow.
In our view this also excludes the possible participation of communities or individuals who might be affected later by a case similar to the one that would now be under consideration by mechanisms established in this bill. The concern is simply that the language of the bill is susceptible to narrow definition in a way which would exclude the participation of people who should have a right to participate in matters concerning the Canadian environment.
There is a danger which we recognize. If the door is open to participation by anyone, there could be a number of frivolous persons wasting the time and money of the taxpayer, and wasting the time of the agencies established here. For that reason we have placed in the amendment the right to exclude the participation of anyone whose reason for wanting to participate can be described as frivolous, vexatious, or as unreasonable behaviour. That is the purpose of the amendment. It speaks not simply to the mechanism of this bill but to the much broader public question of who has a right to participate in proceedings relating to the preservation of the Canadian environment. We are concerned that the bill as it stands limits that right to participate to people with a narrow, legal interest. We want it broadened. We believe this amendment will

achieve that broadening without inviting a flood of frivolous participation.

"Any concerned person" means that the minister will have to appoint a board at great public expense, even if it is clearly not justified. However, as the minister is more likely to be criticized for not appointing a board than for doing so, she will tend to appoint one on notice of receiving an objection, even if it appears frivolous.
Who is to say that a person's objection is unreasonable, frivolous or vexatious? This could lead to serious argument. To some degree it would restrict the rights of the public. Therefore our position is that we cannot accept the amendment.

speechtext:
that Bill C-253, to provide for the establishment of a Canada Sea Coast Conservation Authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Madam Speaker, the purpose of this bill which is entitled "An Act to provide for the establishment of a Canada Sea Coast Conservation Authority" is to preserve for all Canadians the seacoasts of this country on the east, the west, and perhaps even in the Arctic, although at the moment that is not a pressing need.
The object is to protect the beauty of our coastlines and to oversee the conservation for public recreational use of those seacoasts of Canada that are accessible to the general public. In carrying out this objective I feel it is totally essential that a number of things be done.
First, we should carry out an inventory of the seacoasts to determine which are relatively easily accessible to the public, and which have recrational potential. We must determine the cost involved in either acquiring the areas outright or protecting the environment of these desirable seacoast areas.
When I refer to protecting the environment I mean that where there is agricultural land in use we should pay the owner of that land to maintain his land in its present state. If a fisherman is farming as well as fishing we should pay him to leave the land in its existing state instead of selling his plots to somebody who might want to put up poorly designed cottages.
The authority I envisage would be required to collaborate with not only the provinces but, if there were provincial consent, with the municipalities in such provinces. To make the thing work in the way it must if it is to be successful we would require very major citizen involvement through the various local associations such as historical societies, conservation associations, and other local groups who would join the effort to keep these beautiful areas beautiful. The bill allows for a wide variety of collaboration with governments and groups of private citizens.

Sea Coast Conservation Authority
As the bill indicates, it would be useful for such a conservation authority to take over all existing federal Crown sea coast lands. The authority should also be empowered, if it can work out agreement with provincial governments, to take over the provincial Crown sea coast areas. As I suggested earlier, the authority would be albe to enter into agreements with the municipalities concerned, with provincial consent, to assure the existence of whatever local regulations and by-laws are necessary for the kind of environmental and aesthetic protection we seek.
If we do not have the support of the local public in something like this the thing just will not work. All of us who have travelled to the coasts of Canada, and perhaps even more so to the coasts of the United States, will realize what can happen when there is a total lack of planning and a disregard for the original beauty of the sea coast areas. In this case human greed takes over. Private developers and other groups determine what kind of landscape future generations will face, and that is a pretty miserable and awful prospect. This is the situation now being faced by most citizens in the United States along the east coast, and I suspect along the west coast as well, although I have not visited there. I do not want to see the same thing happen here in Canada.
We still have huge areas of coastline that are relatively unspoiled. We have many thousands of miles of coastline that have retained their beauty, and this bill provides one way by which we can prevent the spoilation of what is unquestionably one of our most important heritages.
I hope no one is under the impression from a first glance at the bill that it is designed to create tourist preserves for the benefit of central Canadian tourists to the disadvantage of the local inhabitants of the sea coast areas. To the contrary, it is designed to prevent our sea coast lands falling into the hands of fast-buck operators from central Canada, the United States, and sometimes from outside North America, to the detriment primarily of the local inhabitants, and to the detriment in the long-term of all Canadians who value the beauty of our seascapes.
While the beaches themselves are and always will be public, it is the area immediately behind these beaches with which we must concern ourselves because they are now threatened in many parts of Canada with the same kind of unplanned and unco-ordinated construction which afflicts the road approaches to practically every town and city in North America.
Whether it is thoughtlessly located or designed commercial building, a third-hand house trailer, or a school bus converted to a seasonal or permanent dwelling or even, in some cases, an attractive summer cottage, it all will contribute to the spoilation or our coastal areas if we do not have better control than we have had up until now.
I said earlier that I envisage a situation whereby we would be paying people to leave land in its existing or original state. It would be a situation in which we would indemnify farmers and fishermen adequately in a way that would make it well worth their while to agree to preserve their land in the form in which it is now providing them a living. It is all very well to suggest that we would not prevent anyone making money through the sale of his land

to someone who wishes to build cottages. Individuals have and will continue to have a right to sell land for these purposes, but, in an area of particular scenic beauty we should be prepared to put up the necessary money to make it worthwhile for the owners to preserve the area for future generations rather than sell out to individuals who obviously will benefit from beautiful cottage locations.
If we continue to let this happen in all the beautiful areas of Canada there will not be anything left for the public to enjoy. Unfortunately many of the most picturesque areas have already reached the point where it would be very expensive to back-track and to try to put things where they were 10 or 15 years ago before this movement to our sea coasts really began to take hold. I am encouraged now by the attitude of Canadians toward the preservation of our past.
Certainly when it comes to a public appreciation of the furniture or our past, of the 18th and 19th century produce of Canadian craftsmen, particularly in Nova Scotia, Quebec, and Ontario, there is major public interest. Our museums are promoting this as well as our historical societies, and the historical societies are doing it as well with respect to our early architectural forms. With the exception of a few areas in the centres of Montreal, Quebec City, now Ottawa and a few other areas like Kingston, our governments have not been encouraging the preservation of our architectural heritage. These architectural forms took many generations to evolve and were based on a fantastic amount of thought.
One needs only to be in one of these older homes for a while to realize how much more thought went into them than into any of the homes being built today. While we have been spending all this money preserving the architecture in the centres or our cities we have been ignoring the early architecture of many parts or our sea coast area which is extremely typical of that part of Canada, and which is almost unique in the world because of the combination of the architecture and the building products that were available at that time.
Certain combinations of architecture and material are unique to the east coasts of Canada and the United States. We have done absolutely nothing to encourage the preservation of this. We should be encouraging the use of the architectural forms, which would not cost more, and would blend with the landscape. Yet, we have done nothing in this regard.
The government should consider granting a lower interest rate to encourage people to build the kind of houses which, for example, in Quebec are traditional to a given landscape, and which on the sea coast of Nova Scotia blend into the scenery. Although this would not represent a great expense to the taxpayers it would preserve for future generations a form of scenery which is unique to our country. My God, Madam Speaker, it seems that wherever one goes in this country one sees the same kind of construction, the same kind of houses from Montreal to Vancouver. Where we have uniqueness why should we not provide some encouragement?
This bill provides for collaboration with CMHC and Heritage Canada to evolve programs designed to encourage the use of these original forms of building and material, as well as the colours which characterize these coasts. This
October 31, 1975

would not in the least restrict some of the newest developments in architecture which, because a great deal of thought has been put into them, have evolved forms of buildings which do integrate well with seascapes.
There is no need for anyone to feel in respect of this bill that they would not be allowed to build summer cottages. That would not be the case. I have often repeated that one of the tragedies in this country is that CMHC has never used its power as a lender to require across Canada, wherever it lends money, the kind of planning which involves not only construction but green space, architecture, aesthetics and land use, the kind of planning that maximizes the use of all available technology and knowledge.
We have had the ability to build useful suburbs since the Second World War, and yet most of our suburbs do not and will not stand the test of time. Sure the houses are well built, but the context in which these houses are built is a poorly designed one. There are no pedestrian or bike paths, there are not enough green spaces.
We could have done everything far better with the technology that was available had CMHC imposed the ideas they had. Deliberately government after government did not give CMHC that kind of power. Successive governments felt that it was a constitutional infringement on the powers of the provinces. It has been my view, and still is, that we should use the leverage instruments we have with CMHC to push provinces and municipalities into doing the things which will assure for future generations the kind of living environment which they deserve. We have all the physical assets in terms of landscape beauty that any country could wish for, and yet we are not taking advantage of them. We have the people in this country who are capable of telling us how to do it. Let us give them an opportunity to do it.
I believe that the bill before us will achieve this aim. I know it has found sympathy among officials in two or three government departments, and I hope that hon. members here will see fit to refer the bill to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development so that we can put additional pressure on the government to bring forward a bill similar to this which would provide us with the means to achieve what I hope hon. members will agree is a necessary objective.
