-because there can be no more important thing for us to consider than the importance of preserving all kinds of things in this country, preserving a reasonable economic system, preserving values, and preserving natural resources. But, perhaps more important, we should be preserving the quality of life, and I think that is perhaps what the hon. member intends by this bill.
Sea Coast Conservation Authority
The hon. member mentioned the fact that there seems to be a difficulty in Canada in this kind of preservation in that quite often these things are sacrificed on the altar of profit. I think that he is right to a great extent, that perhaps we had leaned in the direction of sacrificing everything on the altar of profit. However, I would not want to stand in this chamber, representing the interests that I do, and say I am opposed to the operation of the profit motive in our society. Indeed it is the reasonable and enlightened operation of the profit motive that has built this country.
On the other hand the job of legislators, I think, is to find the balance somewhere between the legitimate operation of the profit motive in the business life of the country and the protection of the public interest. That, I think, would be one of the objects of the authority, not to interfere wilfully with the rights of Canadians to pursue what has been traditionally given to us by our heritage-that is the right to own and develop property-but to temper that right in some way with an obligation that is growing, even in the field of private property, the obligation to consider the larger public interest.
This is the difficulty that faces municipalities when they zone property, restricting the right of people to deal in property; it is the right that comes to play before planning boards and commissions of provinces, so they can in fact accomplish within their sphere what is the object of this bill, namely, the preservation and conservation of Canada's sea coast.
The concept of the bill is not new, it has been with us for some time, and I hope I can be forgiven if I refer, in support of this bill, to the excellent work being done in this province by the conservation authorities of Ontario which are analogous in object and intent to what, as I gather from the hon. member's remarks, he would consider for the sea coasts, of Canada.
The Ontario conservation authorities are in fact now engaged in the development of parks for public use, for the travelling public, and for the public who want to go there for rest and relaxation to get away from the hurly burly of life, and in the preservation of the great forest areas and the development of the banks of the rivers. They are involved as well in assuming the title to property for access to the banks of our rivers, lakes and streams, just as I would imagine the hon. member would like his authority to have authority to deal with these in the case of our sea coasts.
The hon. member mentioned the preservation of our past in terms of retaining for the future historical buildings and places. That has been the job of this kind of authority, in all parts of Canada and the best instance within the national capital is the work of the Rideau Valley Conservation Authority at Manotick in their preservation of the Watson Mill and the Dickinson House. I had the privilege of being there for the opening of that institution and I think all hon. members should go there and visit it. I think they would be quite moved by the work of preservation that has been done.
All too often our sea coasts, our river banks, the centres of our towns, the concession roads of our townships where there are things worth preserving in the urban and rural setting, are set aside because we have been too busy to stop

October 31, 1975
Sea Coast Conservation Authority a while and look to see how important these things are to the preservation of our heritage. We have been too concerned with what is ahead rather than looking to the foundation stones upon which our society was built. It is in that sense I think that the hon. member has raised the matter.
The hon. member spoke about the work of historical societies, and I am sure this would fall within the objectives of this bill. I see he is nodding his head in agreement.
I am to have the honour of attending the unveiling ceremony of a historical plaque commemorating the forwarding trade on the St. Lawrence River erected through the auspices of the Grenville Historical Society. In every part of my constituency there is an active group of people willing and able to ensure that the heritage of our past is not forgotten. I think there could be co-operation between groups of that sort and the kind of authority that the hon. member has proposed.
It would not be the first time for the federal government to be involved in such things. The federal government works actively on the preservation of historical places, and that is commendable. The work should be supported in this House and by all members promoting such things within their constituencies.
Fort Wellington at Prescott is in my constituency, and I have always been grateful for the minister's co-operation with the local people in that undertaking. The Department of Transport has co-operated with the local historical society in the preservation of the locks on the Rideau Canal at Merivale.
The National Capital Commission is another example of co-operation. The entire matter is under study by a committee of this House and it is not being treated on any partisan political level. We all hope that machinery will be developed for the consultation between the national government and the local authorities which is so valuable to that committee. It has the grave responsibility for the very things which are the object of this bill as they refer to the sea coasts of Canada.
I am concerned that the economic difficulties which face us in this country mean that projects important in our history and in the spiritual sense and conservation sense will have to be abandoned or delayed. The blame lies with the government for failing to control inflation. As a result, commendable projects such as suggested by the hon. member must be put aside.
In the House yesterday the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) asked members on all sides not to call for programs that needed extra funding because the government intends to cut back, to slice the fat off the estimates by curbing the size of the public service. Many worth-while projects will be set aside as a result, and perhaps this is one of them.
For the last five years in this country we have been tempted to live beyond our means, and now the government says that many of these worthy projects will fall by the wayside. In face of what the President of the Treasury Board said yesterday about cutting back, I do not see how we can honestly support the creation of another bureaucra-
[Mr: Baker (Grenville-Carleton).]
cy such as would be required to carry out the objects of this bill. I think there is general agreement on all sides of the House that the intention of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) for the preservation of those things precious to us is commendable, but surely we cannot support another bureaucracy.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate having some time this afternoon to comment on this bill. I congratulate the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) for his good work, and my friend across the way for his attitude.
As a member of the Standing Committee of Indian Affairs and Northern Development I am interested in this subject, and I have also done research work on the environment as it affects many of the points the hon. member raised. I think all members in the House would support the objectives set out in the bill, mainly the preservation of our sea coast. There may be some difference in approach to these objectives, however. One question is whether the hon. member would want to establish a new authority or use existing authorities and government agencies. At this time of restraints perhaps we should opt for the latter. I hope the hon. member for Laprairie understands that I am not in any way questioning his objectives or viewpoint when I say that there could be cheaper and perhaps more effective ways of accomplishing this.
I am rather concerned about the constitutionality of what is being proposed, but of course I am not a constitutional lawyer. I understand that the management and sale of public lands is in the hands of the provinces, and I agree with the previous speaker that if the provinces owning coastal waters have conservation authorities already, perhaps it would be best to add to their funding in order to accomplish the things that are desired. In Ontario, conservation authorities are involved with municipal councils not only on an input basis but also in the financing of the authority. It seems that in some provinces we already have certain bodies which combine the provincial and municipal arms of government. Perhaps some of the objects set out by the hon. member can be handled that way.
We should not overlook the work of Canada's historical societies. In my riding there is a tremendous new awareness of our historical heritage and many people are involved in identifying and recording matters of historical interest. I, too, spend much time in this way. I should mention Heritage Canada. I am impressed by some of the work they have done in identifying historical areas which are of National significance, and in promoting public awareness.
I think we should be particularly proud of the job that Parks Canada has done. Parks Canada is a well established government agency and has done many of the things about which the hon. member talked. Probably in the past five or six years we have established more new parks in Canada than were established in the previous 50. At least nine parks are coastal in nature. They have been primarily established for the purpose of preserving coastal zones for conservation and recreation purposes.
October 31, 1975

The shoreline protected by these parks is approximately 400 miles long. We have, for example, Pacific Rim National Park, with approximately 70 miles of coastline proposed for inclusion; Auyuittuq, which takes up 112 miles of the Baffin Island coastline. I suggest that there we have some of the most precious coastline left in Canada. In addition, Prince Edward Island parks account for 30 miles, Fundy National Park for 11 miles, Kouchibouguac for 18 miles, Cape Breton Highlands for 11 miles, Forillon for 22 miles, Gros Morne for 70 miles and Terra Nova for 56 miles. I placed these figures on record to indicate the extent to which Parks Canada has established parks in coastal areas. Of course the primary purpose for which the parks were established was that of preserving the coast.
It is also interesting to note the action taken by a number of provinces with jurisdiction over coastal areas. They have ensured that their coastal land stays within Canadian ownership and is not available for sale to non-Canadians who might perhaps develop it for uses not compatible with the aims set out by the hon. member for Laprairie.
I am interested in most of the aims set out by the hon. member, and I am especially interested in preserving many buildings around the sea coast as these obviously are among the oldest in Canada and, architecturally, are some of the most precious in Canada. They should be preserved if possible.
As the hon. member suggested, we must ask who is to pay for these properties to ensure that they will never be sold or used for any purpose except that of history? Once a building or historical site is identified, if it is important to Canadians it ought to be preserved and maintained by the use of already existing agencies. I suggest that the federal government can help in this regard by providing funds on the condition that the aims set out by the hon. member are met. I think the hon. member's aims are worth pursuing.
I spoke for a few minutes this afternoon to congratulate the hon. member for his work on the bill, to say that I agree with its objects, but to suggest that it is not necessary to refer the bill to committee for consideration, as what the hon. member has in mind can be accomplished by agencies already in place.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) for this bill. If ever any kind of bill justifies the retention of private members' hour, it is this kind of bill. It is a good bill, embodying sound principles. As its mover is a government supporter one would expect the bill to commend itself to the government, even though the bill commends itself to the House. But being cautious, the government will allow few private members' bills to be read the second time. I suppose that is understandable, as such caution is a safeguard against badly drafted legislation and the possibility that badly drafted bills will become law. Yet the principle of referring the subject matter of a bill like this to committee for study is commendable and should receive the favourable consideration of the House.
I was interested to note that three hon. members representing land locked constituencies, namely, the hon. member for Laprairie, the sponsor, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), and the hon. member for
Sea Coast Conservation Authority Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne), spoke in favour of preserving the great heritage of Canada's massive coastline, and rightly so. Often people who live near the sea do not appreciate the sea but tend to take its benefits for granted.
The coasts of Canada are a great heritage. The Newfoundland coastline is over 6,000 miles long. Until fairly recently there were 1,300 towns and villages along that massive coastline. I am sorry to say that their number has been reduced, because of the declining inshore fishery and other economic factors favouring centralization, to about 900. Nevertheless, Newfoundland has a magnificent coastline, with its great bays, beautiful fjords, magnificent coastal panoramas, and bird sanctuaries where one will find nesting many of the great sea birds of the world.
The great danger to our coasts, both in the east and the west, and in the Arctic, comes not from the intrusion of man, not from the commercial exploitation of resources. In a sense the chief enemy is the sea itself, the sea which is rapidly becoming polluted. We remember only too well the accident of the tanker Arrow and the consequences of that accident.
Hardly a day goes by without some oil slick being washed up on some shore somewhere in Canada. Where does the oil originate? It comes from the many ships at sea which disobey maritime laws and dump ballast, bunker fuel, etc. at night when detection is almost impossible. The oil is washed ashore as an oil slick and does irreparable damage to the environment. We have not as yet devised technology to clean up this kind of pollution, especially in Canada where the climate is cold. The colder it gets, the more difficult it is for this kind of oil pollution to break down and disappear into the environment. It is a very serious threat. The further north you get, the more complicated and serious it becomes.
We are probably on the eve of another disaster where somewhere at sea a tanker will run ashore, or an oil well that has been sunk and tapped will start to leak. This happened off the coast of California in the Santa Barbara area with disastrous results. It also happened in the Gulf of Mexico and off the coast of Florida. It is a great danger.
One of the things I like about this bill is that it would put into place in Canada an authority which could provide contingency plans which could be brought into force in the event of such a disaster. Imagine the consequences of an accident in the Gulf or the Bay of Fundy on the magnificent beaches of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick. Think of the damage which could be done to these beautiful beaches, some of the finest in the world. It makes us wonder why we do not have such an authority already.
I believe that the hon. member has brought forward a good idea. It is a good bill. The subject matter would provide a standing committee of the House with the necessary vehicle to look into these questions and make recommendations to the government as to the feasibility of putting into place such an authority as is called for in this bill.
With regard to the preservation of some of the architecture on the east and west coasts of Canada, this bill may not meet that kind of situation. The hon. member for
r

Sea Coast Conservation Authority
Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) referred to the great work of historical societies, Heritage Canada, and Parks Canada. I certainly agree they are doing tremendous work in preserving our architectural heritage.
The beaches of Canada belong to all of us. We have an obligation to ensure that they are protected from the kind of pollution which is perhaps most difficult to control, that which comes from without. I refer to tankers that are allowed to operate along our coastlines and in our territorial waters without proper navigational aids, such as was the case with the tanker Arrow. We can pass all the laws to govern pollution that we wish, but it will not prevent these tramp tankers which fly flags of convenience from traversing our coastlines, running the risk of going aground and dumping their cargoes. They not only do irreparable damage to our beaches, but to the fisheries and marine life which find sanctuary within them. This bothers and frightens me.
I love the sea. I was born on the east coast of Canada. I was raised with the sea in my blood. To walk on the clean, wholesome beaches of eastern Canada is a tremendous exercise, a tremendous advantage. I hope that we as a parliament will take steps to put into place some kind of authority, perhaps not exactly as envisaged in the hon. member's bill, but at least set up some kind of authority to preserve this great resource, protecting it from the polluters of this world and ensuring that the quaint villages that are found, especially on the east coast of Canada, are preserved for generations to come. I hope the House will allow the subject matter of the hon. member's bill to go to the committee.
